candidate.description: A village irrigation crew initially coordinates gate openings by passing instructions from person to person. Because each resident can privately recall a particular exchange through at most three subsequent interpersonal exchanges, long conversational chains are unreliable: ordinary conversations can erase an instruction before the required action occurs. The crew therefore reorganizes coordination around the communal inscription room. Instead of recording a detailed sequence of future commands that may become stale, residents use their daily ten-minute visit to inscribe a small set of pending irrigation states: which gate action has most recently been durably confirmed, which action should occur next, and whether a known condition requires the sequence to pause. A resident who reads that the eastern gate is next can perform the action and, if their daily room visit remains available afterward, later inscribe the new confirmed state. Short verbal exchanges still bridge gaps between visits, but any instruction dependent on private recall must be acted upon before more than three subsequent interpersonal exchanges occur. This produces an unexpected coordination rhythm. Progress through a multi-person task is no longer primarily limited by how quickly villagers can talk; it is limited by opportunities to convert transient coordination into persistent shared state. Residents begin conserving their single room visit strategically. Visiting early provides current information but sacrifices the ability to record developments discovered later. Delaying the visit preserves an opportunity to publish a later state change but leaves the resident dependent on short-lived verbal information beforehand. Different roles therefore develop different useful visit timings even without any formal scheduler: residents expected to initiate morning actions benefit from early visits, while those expected to confirm later actions benefit from retaining access until later in the day. The system also favors coordination protocols in which each durable inscription describes the presently confirmed state and a limited next action rather than requiring residents to reconstruct a long conversational history. This does not eliminate gaps. If someone acts after using their daily visit, the completed action may remain absent from the communal inscription until an informed resident with unused access records it, and verbal knowledge of the action can disappear if it is not transferred or acted upon within the recall ceiling. Thus repeated coordination produces a scarce resource that did not exist explicitly in the original arrangement: not merely inscription-room time, but the option value of an unused daily visit. Villagers must coordinate both the irrigation work and when they consume their only opportunity to read and alter durable shared state.

critique.rationale: The candidate respects the constraints separately and develops them into a substantive coordination mechanism. For private recall, no instruction is relied upon beyond three subsequent interpersonal exchanges; expired conversational information is allowed to disappear rather than being silently recovered. For the communal room, each resident retains only one daily ten-minute visit, inscriptions persist, and the candidate explicitly recognizes that using a visit early prevents later consultation or inscription that day. The strongest causal development is the emergence of the unused visit as an option-bearing resource: bounded recall plus one-shot durable access produces incentives to time access according to operational role. The progression from transient communication to persistent state, then to strategic visit timing and state-oriented protocols, goes materially beyond restating the premise. It also provides useful descendant material concerning synchronization, visit-order strategies, stale state, handoffs, and protocol design.
critique.uncertainty: The effectiveness of role-specific visit timing depends on the temporal structure of irrigation work and on whether informed residents with unused visits are available when state changes occur. Branch diversity cannot yet be assessed because only this Coordination candidate is provided.
limitations: The claim that early visitors benefit from early access and later confirmers benefit from delayed access is plausible rather than universal; changing irrigation timing could reverse those incentives.

A resident who reads a next action and performs it cannot necessarily inscribe completion later if reading itself consumed that resident's daily visit; the candidate correctly conditions later inscription on access remaining, but descendants must preserve this distinction.

Present physical gate or water states could sometimes reveal what occurred without conversational recall, reducing dependence on inscription; such observation should not be conflated with a prohibited durable record.
The proposed state-oriented protocol is an emergent adaptation, not a guaranteed solution, and can still produce gaps when actions occur after relevant residents have exhausted their visits.
critique.judgment: Retain as a coherent and generative coordination branch. Its most valuable contribution is identifying daily inscription access as a strategically consumable option whose timing becomes part of the coordination problem itself.

candidate.description: The village uses the communal inscription room to maintain a shared grain ledger. Residents record authorized withdrawals and completed collections during their single daily visit so that later visitors can determine what remains owed. One afternoon, part of the granary roof collapses and exposes several bins to rain. A resident inspecting the damage tells the grain keeper that grain from those bins must be distributed immediately. The keeper has already used the day's room visit and cannot alter the durable ledger until tomorrow. Emergency distribution therefore begins through interpersonal instructions. Initially this works: a resident told to collect a particular quantity can act while that exchange remains privately recallable. But the emergency itself increases conversation. People ask about damaged bins, available containers, household needs, and who has already collected grain. Each interpersonal exchange advances the recall limit for earlier exchanges. Some participants consequently lose the details of their authorization before acting, while others successfully collect grain but later lose the conversational context explaining why their withdrawal differed from the inscription. Residents who still have unused room visits can potentially preserve pieces of the emergency state, but only if they learn those pieces while they remain recallable and reach the room before consuming their own visit. The result is not necessarily total informational collapse; instead, the durable ledger becomes unevenly synchronized with reality. Some emergency withdrawals are recorded by informed residents, some remain absent, and some inscriptions may preserve outcomes without preserving enough context to determine how they relate to the original allocation. As further exchanges occur, missing links can become permanently unrecoverable. The next day, the village may know the physical quantity of grain remaining and possess a persistent ledger containing both old allocations and some emergency updates, yet still be unable to establish a unique history connecting them. Two households can plausibly claim that they were promised the same remaining allocation, with neither claim resolvable from surviving inscriptions and neither claimant able to recall the expired exchange that would settle the matter. The shared arrangement has therefore failed in a deeper way than simple record staleness: its history has become partially non-reconstructible. Restoring operation requires a new authoritative decision about present entitlements rather than discovering with certainty what the previous arrangement required. The village can continue using the inscription room, but the repaired allocation must begin from acknowledged uncertainty, because durable writing made after conversational information disappears cannot recreate details that were never inscribed.

critique.rationale: The candidate is constraint-coherent and develops a strong failure mode. The recall ceiling is handled correctly: each participant's relevant exchange can survive through at most three subsequent interpersonal exchanges, emergency conversation consumes that window, and expired details are not reconstructed from private memory. The communal-room restrictions are separately respected: the keeper cannot revisit after using the daily visit, other residents may use their own unused visits, inscriptions persist, and no additional durable record is introduced. Causal depth is substantial: emergency activity increases communication, which accelerates informational expiry precisely when synchronization is most needed; partial inscription then creates uneven correspondence between durable state and reality, producing non-reconstructible history and forcing prospective reallocation rather than retrospective recovery. That feedback between crisis intensity and memory loss is a useful non-obvious consequence with strong descendant potential.
critique.uncertainty: How much history becomes irrecoverable depends on visit timing, which residents receive which information, and what current physical conditions establish independently of expired conversations. Branch diversity cannot yet be assessed because only this Failure candidate is provided.
limitations: The statement that residents record withdrawals during their daily visit is potentially awkward because a resident who consulted the ledger earlier cannot return to record a later withdrawal; the narrative subsequently recognizes this constraint but the opening description could imply a smoother workflow than is guaranteed.
A counterexample is an informed resident with an unused visit who promptly inscribes enough authorization and withdrawal detail to prevent the disputed history from arising.
Physical grain quantities can establish current inventory but generally cannot establish who received particular withdrawals or why; descendants should maintain that distinction.
The example of two households claiming the same allocation requires some ambiguity in surviving inscriptions and should remain a possible consequence rather than an inevitable one.
critique.judgment: Retain as a causally rich failure branch. Its strongest contribution is the discovery that emergencies can simultaneously increase the need for coordination and accelerate destruction of the transient information needed to synchronize the only durable record.
